Topic: CSCI-569: Seminar in Theory. This catalog entry has student-, instructor-, or term-specific content. Create a rigorous orientation companion that teaches the stable process, standards, planning methods, evaluation criteria, and representative examples without inventing a fixed RIT syllabus. Official catalog description: This course examines current topics in Theory. This is intended to allow faculty to pilot potential new undergraduate offerings. Specific course details (such as prerequisites, course seminar, format, learning outcomes, assessment methods, and resource needs) will be determined by the faculty member(s) who propose a specific seminar course in this area. Specific course instances will be identified as belonging to the Theory cluster, the Security cluster, or both clusters. Contact Hours: Lecture 3 Regeneration revision 2: use ten distinct, specific beat titles and avoid repeating any title or section label.

Source excerpts:

[mit-algorithms]
Algorithm analysis connects a precise problem specification to a correctness argument and resource bounds. Asymptotic notation describes how resource use grows with input size. A loop invariant supports a proof by initialization, maintenance, and termination. Divide-and-conquer algorithms split a problem, solve subproblems, and combine their results. Recurrences describe the cost of recursive algorithms. Graph algorithms operate on vertices and edges to answer reachability, ordering, connectivity, and path questions. Dynamic programming records solutions to overlapping subproblems. Core methods include sorting, hashing, trees, graphs, shortest paths, and dynamic programming. A disciplined solution states inputs and outputs, proves correctness, and then analyzes time and space.

[opendsa]
OpenDSA presents data structures and algorithms through executable visualizations and exercises. Lists represent ordered sequences with position-based operations. Stacks use last-in, first-out access, while queues use first-in, first-out access. Trees represent hierarchical relationships and support recursive traversals. Hash tables map keys to locations and require a collision strategy. Graphs can be represented with adjacency structures for traversal and path algorithms. Automata and formal languages describe machines, accepted strings, and computational limits. Representation choices and invariants determine which operations are efficient and which errors are possible.

This course examines current topics in Theory. This is intended to allow faculty to pilot potential new undergraduate offerings. Specific course details (such as prerequisites, course seminar, format, learning outcomes, assessment methods, and resource needs) will be determined by the faculty member(s) who propose a specific seminar course in this area. beats.claim: This course examines current topics in Theory and is intended to allow faculty to pilot potential new undergraduate offerings.
beats.example: A professor proposes a new undergraduate course in theoretical computer science to test its viability before full adoption.
beats.title: Course Purpose and Faculty Role
beats.visualDirection: Display a slide with the course title and a brief description of the faculty proposal process.

beats.claim: Specific course instances will be identified as belonging to the Theory cluster, the Security cluster, or both clusters.
beats.example: A proposed course on cryptographic protocols is classified under the Security cluster, while a course on computational complexity falls under the Theory cluster.
beats.title: Course Classification Clusters
beats.visualDirection: Show a Venn diagram with two overlapping circles labeled 'Theory Cluster' and 'Security Cluster', with a third circle labeled 'Both Clusters' in the intersection.

beats.claim: Specific course details, such as prerequisites, course seminar, format, learning outcomes, assessment methods, and resource needs, will be determined by the faculty member(s) who
beats.example: The proposing faculty member sets the prerequisite to include discrete mathematics and defines the format as a three-hour weekly lecture.
beats.title: Faculty-Determined Details
beats.visualDirection: List the specific course details (prerequisites, seminar, format, learning outcomes, assessment methods, resource needs) with checkboxes for faculty to fill in.

beats.claim: The stable process for piloting new undergraduate courses involves faculty proposal, cluster identification, and detailed planning.
beats.example: The department follows a standardized workflow: faculty submit a proposal, assign cluster(s), define details, and pilot the course.
beats.title: Stable Process Overview
beats.visualDirection: Create a linear flowchart with four steps: Proposal Submission, Cluster Assignment, Detail Planning, and Course Pilot.

beats.claim: Course design standards require clear learning outcomes and assessment methods tailored to the proposed topic.
beats.example: The learning outcomes specify that students will analyze algorithmic correctness and resource bounds, assessed through a final theoretical proof assignment.
beats.title: Standards for Course Design
beats.visualDirection: Display a table with columns for 'Learning Outcome' and 'Assessment Method', filled with example entries.

beats.claim: Resource needs must be identified and documented as part of the course planning process.
beats.example: The faculty member lists required resources, including a whiteboard, projection system, and specific textbooks on theoretical computer science.
beats.title: Planning Methods for Resources
beats.visualDirection: Show a checklist graphic with items like 'Whiteboard', 'Projection System', 'Textbooks', and 'Online Resources' for faculty to mark.

beats.claim: Evaluation criteria for faculty proposals must assess alignment with cluster standards and feasibility of the pilot course.
beats.example: The proposal is evaluated based on whether it meets Theory cluster standards and whether the proposed resources are sufficient for a successful pilot.
beats.title: Evaluation Criteria for Proposals
beats.visualDirection: Create a rubric with criteria: 'Cluster Alignment', 'Feasibility', 'Learning Outcomes', and 'Resource Availability', with scoring scales.

beats.claim: Representative examples of Theory cluster courses include topics like algorithm analysis, data structures, and formal languages.
beats.example: A sample Theory cluster course covers loop invariants, divide-and-conquer algorithms, and graph reachability.
beats.title: Representative Examples of Theory Courses
beats.visualDirection: List three example course titles with brief descriptions: 'Introduction to Algorithm Analysis', 'Data Structures and Algorithms', 'Formal Languages and Automata'.

beats.claim: Faculty must apply the stable process and evaluation criteria to finalize their course proposal before pilot implementation.
beats.example: The faculty member reviews the proposal against the evaluation criteria, makes necessary adjustments, and submits the final plan for departmental approval.
beats.title: Application to Course Planning
beats.visualDirection: Show a before-and-after comparison of a course proposal document, highlighting changes made based on evaluation criteria.

beats.claim: A practical analysis checklist ensures all course details, cluster classifications, and evaluation criteria are met before the pilot begins.
beats.example: The checklist includes items like 'Proposal submitted', 'Cluster assigned', 'Details defined', 'Resources secured', 'Evaluation criteria met', and 'Pilot approved'.
beats.title: Practical Analysis Checklist
beats.visualDirection: Display a printable checklist graphic with checkboxes for each item, ready for faculty to use during the planning phase.
